sections.heading: Highlights
sections.text:
Sn/f-Cu electrode was prepared by electroplating Sn catalyst on Cu foam substrate. Sn/f-Cu electrode is used as cathode for electrocatalytic reduction of CO2. Average current density can reach to ~8 mA cm−2 during CO2 electrolysis. Sn/f-Cu electrode shows excellent performance for reduction of CO2 to formate.

Abstract Sn/f-Cu electrode has been prepared by electrodeposition Sn on a Cu foam substrate in aqueous plating solution, which has been used as the cathode for electrochemical reduction of carbon dioxide (CO2) in aqueous KHCO3 solution. Here, we have explored the effects of the deposition time and the electrolysis potential on the faradaic efficiency for producing formate. The results demonstrate that maximum faradaic efficiency of 83.5% is obtained at −1.8 V vs. Ag/AgCl when the Sn/f-Cu electrode is prepared by electrodeposition for 35 min. The Sn/f-Cu electrode exhibits excellent catalytic activity for CO2 reduction compared with the Cu foam electrode and the Sn plate electrode. The average current density and the production rate of formate for the Sn/f-Cu electrode are more than twice those for the Sn plate electrode during electrochemical reduction of CO2. Keywords: Tin; Electrodeposition; Copper foam; Electrocatalytic reduction; Carbon dioxide; Formate

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
As a leading cause of global warming, carbon dioxide (CO2) is easily formed during
combustion or respiration. Electrochemical or photoelectrochemical reduction of CO2 could provide an attractive solution to this climate issue, with CO2 converted into useful fuels and utilized as a chemical feedstock [1-3]. It is also an energy storage strategy, with solar or electrical energy stored as chemical energy in a reduced carbon product [4]. In recent years, considerable attempts have been made to find a feasible technology to convert CO2 into useful chemicals [5-7]. Among the findings of these researches, one attractive option is to convert CO2 into formic acid or formate (depending on pH). Formic acid is a fundamental chemical which is widely used in the textile industry, tanning industry, rubber processing industry, and pharmaceutical industry [8]. It can also function as an energy material, as it can be used in direct formic acid fuel cell to produce electricity [9, 10].
A number of homogeneous and heterogeneous catalysts have been evaluated for
electrochemical CO2 reduction, especially metals [11-13]. Metal electrodes were the traditional electrodes due to their excellent performance for electrochemical reduction of CO2. Among these metal electrodes, Cu electrode is a commonly used electrode for electrochemical reduction of CO2 [14-17]. For improve the catalytic performance of the Cu electrode, researchers have developed many novel construction types, including Cu nanofoams [18], Cu nanoparticles [19], nanoporous Cu [20] and Cu alloys [21]. These reports have greatly enriched the types of the electrodes used for electrochemical reduction of CO2. And the novel electrodes have bigger specific surface areas which can provide more active sites to accelerate the electrochemical reaction, whereas, these Cu-based electrodes have low product selectivity to formate in aqueous electrolytes [22]. Qiao J L et al. had explored an effective fibrous Cu electrode surface, created using a procedure combining
Page 5 of 23

M an

4
high-temperature annealing and electroreduction, for CO2 reduction to produce HCOO −, and the highest faradaic efficiency obtained was ~43% [23]. Sen S et al. had reported the electrochemical reduction of CO2 on copper foam with hierarchical porosity, and found that the highest faradaic efficiency for producing HCOOH was 29% [18]. Unlike Cu, Sn is an excellent catalyst for electrochemical reduction of CO2 to formate in aqueous solutions, and the faradaic efficiency can easily achieve above 80% at the appropriate electrolysis conditions [24]. It is necessary to develop an electrode that can integrate the properties of Sn with high catalytic activity and special structured Cu substrate with big specific surface area, and the target electrode will possess high selectivity and high production rate of formate. Such electrode can be prepared by electrodeposition which is a facile, timesaving and low-cost method [25].
In this article, Sn was deposited on Cu foam substrate by electrodeposition in aqueous plating
solution, which was employed as a cathode for electrochemical reduction of CO2 with the aim to obtain big catalytic current density and high production rate of formate.

sections.heading: 2.1. Preparation of Sn/f-Cu electrode
sections.text:
Cu foam (thickness 1 mm) was firstly treated by acid pickling, then ultrasonically cleaned with
ethanol and deionized water which was conducted to remove the industrial oil, dried with flowing air. Lastly the obtained copper foam was used as the substrate for electrochemical deposition. The electrochemical deposition was performed on the Cu substrate in aqueous electrolytic solution. Sodium citrate was first dissolved in deionized water to form a 0.05 mol L−1 solution, and the resulting pH was adjusted to 6 with H2SO4. Then SnCl2 was added to the above solution and its concentration was 0.018 mol L−1. The solution was moderately stirred at least 10 h before
Page 6 of 23
Ac ce
pt ed
M an
us cr
ip t
5
electroplating process commencement. Agitation was kept on within the electroplating process. Sn-based film was deposited on the Cu substrate by galvanostatic electroplating at 4.8 mA for different times. The final deposits were sequentially rinsed with methanol and deionized water, and the sample obtained was marked as Sn/f-Cu. 2.2. Electrochemical experiments
The electrochemical experiments were performed in a conventional three-electrode system with
an undivided glass cell in which an Ag/AgCl electrode (sat. KCl) was chosen as the reference electrode and a Pt plate (2 cm2) was chosen as the counter electrode. The Sn/f-Cu with the geometric surface area of 1 cm2 was using as the working electrode. The electrolyte used was 40 mL of 0.1 mol·L−1 KHCO3 aqueous solution. All experiments were performed under room temperature (20 ± 3 °C) and ambient pressure.
Linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) was performed with a CHI 660D electrochemical workstation
(Shanghai Chenhua Instruments Co., Ltd., China) in electrolyte after being bubbled with N2 or CO2 for 30 min at a scan rate of 0.05 V s−1. The current density (j) is determined on the geometrical area of the electrode (1 cm2).
Controlled potential electrolysis was carried out using a LAND CT2001C cell
performance-testing instrument (Wuhan Electronics Co., Ltd., China). The electrolyte was saturated with CO2 before each electrolysis process, and CO2 gas was continuously aerated at a flow rate of 20 mL min−1 during the electrolysis process. The electrolysis experiments were terminated when the amount of charge passed reached to 40 C. The average current density (ja) is expressed as the total current divided by the geometric area of the electrode (1 cm2) for all cells. 2.3. Analysis and calculations

Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and energy dispersion spectroscopy (EDS) were obtained
on a Hitachi S-4800 at an acceleration voltage of 15 kV. X-ray diffraction pattern (XRD) was recorded on a Bruker D8 Focus diffractometer using Cu Kα radiation (λ = 1.54056 Å), scan range from 25 to 80 °.
The products in the electrolyte were directly analyzed by an ion chromatography instrument
(Dionex ICS-900) equipped with IonPac AS11-HC (250 mm × 4 mm) and AG11-HC (50 mm × 4 mm) columns. 0.03 mol L−1 KOH solution was used for isocratic elution, and leaching rate was 1 mL min −1. 10 µL of the sample were used for each time.
The faradaic efficiency for producing formate (f) is determined by equation (1):
f = 2nF / Q (1)
where the 2 represents the number of electrons required for the formation of one molecule of formate from CO2; n is the moles of the formate produced; F is Faraday’s constant (96485 C mol −1 of electrons); and Q is the amount of charge in Coulomb passed across the electrode during the electrolysis (Q = 40 C here). 3. Results and discussion
Fig. 1 shows the faradaic efficiencies for electrochemical reduction of CO2 to formate on the
Sn/f-Cu electrodes which are prepared at different deposition times. It can be seen that the faradaic efficiency for producing formate increases as the deposition time increases until 35 min, where it reaches to the maximum. When the electrode is prepared by deposition in a short time, the Sn coating may be not fully covered on the surface of the Cu foam substrate which leads to low faradaic efficiency for CO2 reduction. And we can see that the faradic efficiency decreases slightly when the deposition time is longer than 35 min. Therefore, the Sn/f-Cu electrodes were prepared by

electrodeposition for 35 min in the following experiments.
Figs. 2a and 2b give the morphologies of the Cu foam and the Sn/f-Cu electrode. It can be seen
that the Cu foam has the microporous structure (Fig. 2a). As shown in Fig. 2b, for the Sn/f-Cu electrode, Sn particles are deposited on the surface of the Cu foam and the significant dendrites are present on the joints of the Cu foam after deposition of Sn (Fig. 2b). Fig. 2c shows the SEM image of the structure details of the Sn/f-Cu electrode, it can be seen that the surface of the Sn/f-Cu electrode is fully covered by the grain-like Sn particles with a mean diameter of around 500 nm, which could be cnsidered that the Sn layer is around 500 nm thick. The Sn peaks appear in the EDS spectrum of the Sn/f-Cu electrode (Fig. 2d). The results from Fig. 2 indicate that Sn has been coated on Cu foam substrate successfully.
Fig. 3 gives the XRD patterns of the Cu foam and the Sn/f-Cu electrode. The peaks at 43.5, 50.6,
and 74.2 ° are assigned to (111), (200) and (220) planes of the copper foam substrate (PDF card no. 65-9743), respectively. For the Sn/f-Cu electrode, except the diffraction peaks of Cu, other main peaks at 30.8, 32.2, 44.1 and 45.1 ° are assigned to (200), (101), (220) and (211) planes of the deposited Sn (PDF card no. 4-673). It shows that the Sn catalyst has been deposited on the surface of the Cu foam, which is consistent with the analytical result of Fig. 2.
In order to investigate the effect of electrolysis potential on electrochemical reduction of CO2,
the electrolysis experiments were carried out at different electrolysis potentials range from −1.5 to −1.9 V. Fig. 4 shows the variations of the electrolysis current density with electrolysis time during the electrochemical reduction of CO2 at different electrolysis potentials. The electrolysis current density increases as the electrolysis potential decreases from −1.5 to −1.9 V, and it remains almost un-changed at each electrolysis potential, which may mean that the nature of the cathodic reaction is

not changed. And the electrolysis current density is fluctuant at more negative potentials (especialy −1.9 V), which can be explained by a lot of bubbles producing due to the hydrogen evolution reaction.
Fig. 5 shows the faradaic efficiencies and the average current densities for electrochemical
reduction of CO2 to formate on the Sn/f-Cu electrodes at different electrolysis potentials. The average current density increases as the electrolysis potential decreases, which is in agreement with the results of Fig. 4. It can be seen from Fig. 5 that the faradaic efficiency for producing formate increases as the electrolytic potential decreases from −1.5 to −1.8 V. As the potential further decreases to −1.9 V, the faradaic efficiency decreases, this can be attributed to the enhancement of H2 evolution at more negative electrolysis potentials. It can be concluded that the maximum faradaic efficiency of 83.5% is obtained by electrochemical reduction of CO2 at the electrolysis potential of −1.8 V.
Fig. 6 depicts the LSV curves of the copper foam electrode, the Sn plate electrode and the
Sn/f-Cu electrode in 0.1 mol L−1 KHCO3 solutions after being bubbled with N2 or CO2 for 30 min. At more negative potentials, sharp increases of the current densities can be observed under both N2 and CO2. Under N2, this increase is due to the reduction of H2O (hydrogen evolution reaction) [26, 27]; under CO2, the enhanced current must be caused by the reduction of both H2O and CO2:
2H+ + 2e → H2 (3) CO2 + H + + 2e → HCOO− (4)
For the Cu foam electrode, no large difference is found in the reduction current densities under N2 and under CO2, which can be explained by the strong hydrogen evolution reaction greatly inhibiting CO2 reduction reaction on the Cu foam electrode. It also can be found that, the reduction current

density under N2 for the Sn/f-Cu electrode is obviously lower than that for the Cu foam electrode, which shows that Sn coating on the Cu foam can effectively inhibit hydrogen evolution reaction. For both the Sn plate electrode and the Sn/f-Cu electrode, the reduction current densities under N2 are lower than those under CO2 obviously. It indicates that the Sn plate electrode and the Sn/f-Cu electrode have excellent catalytic activities toward CO2 reduction, especially for the Sn/f-Cu electrode which shows higher reduction current density. The above results indicate that the Sn coating on the Cu foam can improve the performance for electrochemical reduction of CO2 effectively.
We also carried out the electrolysis experiments on the Cu foam electrode and the Sn plate
electrode at −1.8 V in CO2-saturated 0.1 mol L −1 KHCO3 solutions, the electrolysis results are shown in Fig. 7. It can be found that, for the Cu foam electrode, the Sn plate electrode and the Sn/f-Cu electrode, the faradaic efficiencies for producing formate are 18%, 81.7% and 83.5%, respectively; the average current densities for electrolysis are 12.63, 3.21 and 7.56 mA cm−2, respectively; the production rates for electrochemical reduction of CO2 to formate are 42.4, 48.9 and 118 µmol h −1, respectively. For the Cu foam electrode, the average current density is high, whereas the faradaic efficiency and the production rate of formate are low compared with the Sn plate electrode and the Sn/f-Cu electrode. For the Sn/f-Cu electrode, the faradaic efficiency for producing formate is a little higher than that of the Sn plate electrode, whereas the average current density and the production rate of formate are more than twice those of the Sn plate electrode. It can be concluded that the Sn/f-Cu electrode is an excellent electrode for electrochemical reduction of CO2 to formate.
From this work, it indicates that the catalyst can be decorated on the porous substrate through
the method of electrodeposition, and the prepared composite electrode can exhibit the performances

of the deposited catalyst and the substrate. In this way, more functional electrodes can be developed and used for CO2 reduction. 4. Conclusions
Sn/f-Cu electrode has been prepared by electrodeposition Sn on a Cu foam substrate in a
sodium citrate aqueous electrolyte containing SnCl2. The morphology and structure of the Sn/f-Cu electrode are characterized by SEM, EDS and XRD. The results indicate that Sn particles are loaded on the Cu foam substrate successively. Furthermore, the Sn/f-Cu electrode is used as the cathode for electrochemical reduction of carbon dioxide (CO2) in aqueous KHCO3 solution. Faradaic efficiency for producing formate is influenced by the deposition time and the electrolysis potential. When the electrolysis is carried out at the optimum conditions, that is, the electrolysis is carried out at −1.8 V vs. Ag/AgCl on the Sn/f-Cu electrode prepared by deposition for 35 min, the average current density can reach up to ~8 mA cm−2 and the faradaic efficiency for producing formate can reach to 83.5%. The Sn/f-Cu electrode shows excellent performance for electrochemical reduction of CO2 to formate compared with the Cu foam and the Sn plate.
